en: To torture him and bring calamity,
To spare not a hair of the villain,
But torment him and take his life;
To face whatever fate might bring,
And stand as a protecting presence
Beside her son, the falcon-warrior.
Your mother Kanykey ran,
Flying like an arrow in her joy,
Toward Khan Kanchoro’s horde,
Ready as a hawk.
Inspiration came to her from the unseen;
She weighed her wits and pondered:
“I shall seize and slaughter Kanchoro,
And roast the bitch Chachykey
For my feast,
Then put an end to the grievous misery
And all the humiliations I have suffered.”
The old guards blocking the road
Threw everything down in ruin,
Even the bravest among them.
The hard-pressed guards fled,
Scattering their swords on the ridge;
Bellowing and stumbling,
Many souls fled back.
When they heard of the hero’s courage,
The sentries ran away.
The many guards scattered in panic
And reached their separate homes,
Abandoning all their possessions;
The swaggering champions
Fled each to his own place.
“The hero’s son has come,” they said,
“The apple of Külchoro’s eye;
The bloodthirsty hero’s own young champion,
For whose feast ninety beasts were slaughtered,
Who was named Seytek—
The noble one himself has come!”
They swiftly invoked Baabedin,
Having heard he was the consummate champion.
They heard that divinely protected Külchoro
And hero Seytek had come.
The champions who had heard of them before
Invoked God and slaughtered sheep,
Shouting approval and slaughtering colts,
And began a mighty celebration.
They left Kanchoro’s gate
Deserted and unguarded.
They passed it contemptuously;
The gatekeepers at the outer entrance,
The keepers of the khan’s door,
The warriors stationed on watch,
And the brave sentries—
Every one of them fled.
The people raised a clamorous uproar
And had long since reached
The very seat of Kanchoro.
Her champion and protector
Had been wounded in sixty places.
The blue mountain pass had become a marsh;
Little true valor remained
Of that lineage now exhausted.
Few of the bloodline remained;
Most of my son’s strength was gone.
“May that roaring madman
Not suddenly bring humiliation upon him.
While my hair is white as down,
As he sets out upon his journey,
At the hour when he cannot turn back,
Now that the end draws near,
Let me die before fate claims me;
For my son, small as a crow,
Let me grapple and spill his enemy’s blood.”
To inflict the utmost torment,
And rescue divinely protected Külchoro
From the furious swine’s clutches,
She hastened onward.
What had been spoken early now seemed late;
Her two eyes strained in longing,
Her knees crackled as they bent,
Yet summoning her courage, she ran.
How could she hold herself back?
She leaned upon the sharp Albar sword
Given by Atash;
How could this grief-stricken old woman
Possibly spare herself
From the dragon’s affliction?
Following Aichürök,
The venerable white-haired Kanykey,
His mother, arrived.
With a protector, one’s belly is full;
Apart from one’s mother, there is no Mecca.
His mother had arrived,
And beside his protector
His beloved had arrived.
Külchoro saw his mother and sister-in-law,
He saw his dearest ones.
When the venerable women came,
His body turned cold and trembled,
And his wretched life, merely held in trust,
Started from his crown and shrieked.
Finding no place to make a stand,
He despaired of his fly-like life;
Not a trace of life remained in him.
His voice deserted his throat,
His last owl-like feather fell,
And he stood disheveled in anguish,
Thus despairing of life.
His whole body shuddered
When he saw Külchoro and Kanykey
Together with Aichürök;
The wretch found no recourse,
And his tiny soul screamed.
He flew from the throne
And crashed upon the ground.
His head struck the earth,
And split open
A full span and two fingers wide.
The oath-breaker was struck by his oath,
The accursed was struck by a demon,
Struck by the dust of the white horses,
Struck by the glory of his father Manas,
Struck by the strength of Semetey,
Struck by Kanykey’s milk.
The warrior lay there, struck by his oath.
The accursed was struck by a demon,
Struck by the bloom of the white fruit,
Struck by the days of kumis and nights of maidens,
Struck by the mighty age of the Kyrgyz.
As Kanchoro stood there thus,
Kanykey and Aichürök
Rose together in equal fury
And addressed Kanchoro.
Speaking softly but striking hard,
Kanykey entered and began:
“Yesterday, when my son Semetey
Was left fatherless,
His mother carried him away in flight.
Deprived of his champions,
That son of a bitch, that swine,
That hero who troubled the world,
That infidel who spread seductive turmoil,
Was deserted by the retinue at his side
And left sitting thus.
His guards fled and his strength departed,
The watchmen beside him were gone;
He had no champions and no khan.
All the fierce men who would swarm
At a single command were gone.
However loudly he shouted and cried,
He had neither support nor strength,
No stronghold from which to shoot,
No khan to serve as protector,
And none of the courageous heroes.
He burned fiercely in grief,
And was parted from the wife
Who had been his protector,
Leaving him alone in the horde.
The two women and Külchoro
Prepared to punish the villain who ruined the people,
The wild-headed instigator of strife,
The great lord known throughout the age,
The fiercely wrathful destroyer,
The slayer of so many heroes—
They would make the staggering lord,
The great Kanchoro,
Pay the penalty.
Kanykey and Chürök burned with grief;
Wretched Kanchoro
Despaired of his precious life.
Courage left his heart,
Strength left his wrists,
Tears fell from his lashes;
Wayward Kanchoro
Lost all his power.
His heart burning and his insides boiling,
Like a wolf caught in their hands,
He stared wildly, his two eyes glaring.
Your fortunes rose ever higher;
Your sheep shared the same fold,
Your feasts the same companions,
Your gains were amassed together,
And you were a peer of my brother the khan.
In the herd-rich Sary-Özön
You took so much land as your portion;
You took the prosperous Kyrgyz people,
Then went and conquered Afghanistan.
My children, wherever your hands reached,
How could Margalan remain unharmed?
You reached and took Afghanistan—
How could Jet-Kayt remain unharmed?
You went scouting together,
You faced death together,
And went among the people as khans.
Yet while among the Kalmyks, you yourself
Pissed into the common cauldron.
You are the black fiend himself,
The very eye of the troublemaker
Who devastates the land and corrupts the people.
Scorched and blazing,
You are the very face of such wickedness.
Yesterday, when I saw you as a child
And gave you my left breast,
Life nearly left my wretched body;
As you sucked at my breast,
Blood flowed from the left nipple.
My whole body turned cold,
My twelve limbs ached,
And my ribs seemed shattered.
As you suckled, my breast
Was split into six pieces.
The humiliation you would bring in the end,
You beastlike, gaunt old vulture,
Was already revealed then.
This child looked different in form
And bore an enemy’s malice within,
But my son would not heed my words.
My dull, blind-hearted son—
When Karakhan fled there,
He grew up as an orphan,
Somehow rejoined the people,
Came of age and became a man,
And stood equal with heroes’ sons.
When he stirred up the great conflict—
To tell what followed would raise a mighty clamor—
Külchoro, descended from Almambet,
And Kanchoro, descended from hero Chubak,
Were taken as spoils by the forty companions
When the forty warriors were slaughtered.
Because of what had been done in that slaughter,
After the carnage among the multitude,
Calling you “banners fixed upon the sword,”
He brought you two sons of bitches
Home as gifts.
He split the rich cuts of meat and fat
And fed them to you;
He made the whole Kyrgyz host and the many Argyn
Ask where the two boys were.
He planted and tended you like trees,
Built you a house and sheltered you,
And laid your mortal enemies low.
Into the great horde with its sharp-tipped roof
He admitted you both as twins.
He fondly mounted you
On steeds no lasso could catch.
He fed you delicacies you had never tasted,
And, saying, “You shall be inseparable brothers,”
I offered both my breasts, right and left,
And suckled the two of you.
He led you with him and made you warriors,
Making you equal to heroes’ sons.
He cherished and raised you both,
Made you full-grown lions,
And brought your fortunes to perfection.
Calling you two brothers from one nest,
Steeds that would not tire riding to Altai,
Iron-hoofed coursers,
